reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Shields' Textbook of Glaucoma
clinicalPearls: A form of open-angle glaucoma with characteristic glaucomatous optic-nerve cupping and visual field loss despite intraocular pressure that remains within the statistically normal range
The optic disc often shows more focal notching, acquired pits, and a higher frequency of splinter disc haemorrhages at the neuroretinal rim than typical high-pressure glaucoma
Field defects tend to be deeper, more localised, and closer to fixation, so central vision may be threatened earlier
Vascular dysregulation is common, with associations such as migraine, Raynaud phenomenon, nocturnal hypotension, and obstructive sleep apnoea
Diagnosis requires excluding secondary and previously higher-pressure causes, including diurnal pressure spikes missed on single readings and thin corneas that underestimate true pressure
Management still centres on lowering intraocular pressure, since a substantial pressure reduction slows progression even when the baseline pressure appears normal
A disc haemorrhage is an important warning sign of ongoing damage and warrants closer monitoring or intensified treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Normal tension glaucoma is a progressive optic neuropathy showing the structural and functional hallmarks of glaucoma while intraocular pressure stays within the normal statistical range. Damage is thought to arise from a combination of pressure-dependent stress on a susceptible optic nerve head and pressure-independent factors, particularly impaired optic-nerve blood flow from vascular dysregulation, systemic and nocturnal hypotension, and possibly a low cerebrospinal-fluid pressure that increases the translaminar pressure gradient. The result is loss of retinal ganglion cells and their axons, producing focal rim thinning, disc haemorrhages, and corresponding nerve-fibre-bundle field defects that often lie nearer fixation than in high-pressure disease.
additionalDifferentials: Primary open-angle glaucoma with unrecognised pressure spikes or thin corneas
Previously elevated (burnt-out) glaucoma such as a resolved pressure-raising episode
Compressive or infiltrative optic neuropathy mimicking glaucomatous cupping
Ischaemic optic neuropathy with pallor and field loss
Congenital optic disc anomalies such as pits or colobomas
Old optic neuritis or other non-glaucomatous optic atrophy
additionalInvestigations: Diurnal intraocular pressure phasing to detect peaks missed on isolated measurements
Central corneal thickness measurement to correct apparent pressure readings
OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer and ganglion cell complex to quantify structural loss
Automated perimetry to characterise and monitor field defects near fixation
Neuroimaging when disc pallor, atypical field loss, or rapid progression suggests a non-glaucomatous cause
Assessment for vascular risk factors including blood pressure profile and sleep apnoea when indicated
redFlags: Optic disc pallor out of proportion to cupping or field loss respecting the vertical midline, suggesting a compressive or neurological cause needing imaging
Rapidly progressive field loss despite apparently normal pressure
Recurrent disc haemorrhages signalling continued optic-nerve damage
Central or paracentral defects threatening fixation and reading vision
reference.prognosis: Many eyes progress slowly, and lowering intraocular pressure substantially reduces the rate of visual field deterioration, but a subset with marked vascular dysregulation or recurrent disc haemorrhages progress despite treatment and risk central visual loss.
pitfalls: Withholding treatment because the pressure looks normal, ignoring evidence of progression
Missing diurnal pressure spikes or overestimating true pressure in eyes with thick corneas and underestimating it in thin corneas
Failing to image the brain and orbit when disc or field features are atypical for glaucoma
Overlooking nocturnal hypotension, sometimes iatrogenic from evening antihypertensives, as a driver of progression
Interpreting any normal-pressure cupping as glaucoma without excluding neurological causes
